title: Red Eye Emergency

patient.name: Mdm Wong Siew Lin
patient.presenting_complaint: Sudden severe right eye pain with headache and vomiting for 4 hours

history.hpc: Mdm Wong presents to the eye casualty at 10pm with sudden onset right eye pain that started 4 hours ago after watching television in a dimly lit room. The pain is severe (8/10), associated with frontal headache, nausea, and two episodes of vomiting. She reports seeing rainbow-coloured haloes around lights. Vision in the right eye is markedly blurred. Left eye is asymptomatic.
history.pmhx: Hypertension on atenolol, no prior eye conditions, no previous episodes
history.social_hx: Lives with son in HDB flat, non-smoker, non-drinker

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Right: conjunctival injection, corneal oedema with epithelial microcysts, shallow anterior chamber (Van Herick grade 1), mid-dilated fixed pupil at 5mm, poor red reflex. Left: shallow anterior chamber (Van Herick grade 2), clear cornea.

fundus.right: Difficult to visualise due to corneal oedema
fundus.left: Normal disc, flat macula, no peripheral changes

investigations.gonioscopy: Right: closed angle on indentation gonioscopy (Shaffer grade 0). Left: narrow angle (Shaffer grade 1-2) — prophylactic LPI indicated.
investigations.axial_length: Right: 21.8mm, Left: 21.6mm — short axial length consistent with hypermetropic eyes predisposed to angle closure

diagnosis: Acute primary angle-closure attack, right eye

immediate: Lie patient supine to allow lens to fall posteriorly
Topical: timolol 0.5% + brimonidine 0.2% + pilocarpine 2% (miotic to open angle) to right eye stat
Oral/IV: acetazolamide 500mg stat (IV if vomiting prevents oral intake)
Analgesia: IV morphine or oral paracetamol for pain
Reassess IOP in 1 hour — target below 30 mmHg to proceed with laser
follow_up: Once IOP controlled and cornea clears: Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) to right eye
Prophylactic LPI to left eye at same or subsequent sitting (narrow angle at risk)
Long-term: monitor for IOP elevation and glaucomatous damage
If IOP remains uncontrolled despite medical therapy: emergency surgical iridectomy
patient_education: Avoid dim lighting and pupil-dilating medications (antihistamines, antidepressants)
Inform family members — first-degree relatives should be screened
LPI is curative for the angle-closure mechanism but glaucoma damage is irreversible
Seek emergency care immediately if symptoms recur in either eye

key_points: Asks about onset and precipitating factors (dim light, prone position, mydriatics)
Family history of angle closure or narrow angles
Medication history — drugs that dilate pupils (antihistamines, antidepressants, anticholinergics)
Requests gonioscopy to confirm angle closure
Assesses fellow eye for narrow angles
Asks about axial length or biometry
Correctly identifies acute angle-closure attack (not open-angle glaucoma)
Initiates emergency IOP-lowering: topical agents + systemic acetazolamide
Includes pilocarpine to constrict pupil and mechanically open angle
Plans laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) as definitive treatment
Addresses prophylactic LPI to fellow eye
